literal: As a state Liao neighbored Liang, Tang, Jin, Han, Zhou, and Song.
idiomatic: Liao bordered in turn Liang, Tang, Jin, Han, Zhou, and Song.

literal: Jin began as father and son in one household because of favor, yet ended with raiding and mutual attack;
idiomatic: With Later Jin the bond began as kin-by-grace yet closed in mutual raids;

literal: Liang, Tang, and Zhou were plainly one enemy state each.
idiomatic: Liang, Tang, and Zhou each stood as a full rival power.

literal: Song only in Taizong's northern Han campaign did Liao fail to save them; most other clashes ended in defeat, and even victories did not repay the cost.
idiomatic: Only when Song's Taizong attacked Northern Han could Liao not relieve the target; otherwise Liao mostly lost, and wins rarely paid for themselves.

literal: This truly stemmed from Shi Jingtang's cession of territory and China's loss of the five passes' natural strength.
idiomatic: The root cause was Shi Jingtang's land grant and the Central States' forfeiture of the five passes' natural defenses.

literal: Goryeo was a small state yet repeatedly cost Liao armies—was it not because its terrain was hard to rely on?
idiomatic: Small Goryeo still drained Liao forces again and again—perhaps its rugged ground alone could explain it.

literal: Western Xia was a tiny realm yet defeated Song in the south and resisted Liao in the east.
idiomatic: Western Xia, though minute, beat Song to the south and held Liao at bay in the east.

literal: Though northwestern horses and warriors were strong, Yuanhao and Liangzuo were surpassingly clever and brave, enabling Tangut and Zubu forces to check a great power—surely mountains and rivers at their backs helped their momentum.
idiomatic: Even with strong northwestern cavalry, Yuanhao and Liangzuo's talent let Tangut and Zubu allies tie down a great empire, aided by mountains and rivers at their flank.

literal: Even so, Song long lacked terrain advantage, yet the old Monograph on troops treated Song alone as the enemy.
idiomatic: Yet Song had lost terrain for years while older records still framed warfare chiefly against Song.

literal: Crossing three passes and massing councils at Beijing, they still dared not advance lightly.
idiomatic: Even after crossing the three passes and gathering councils at Beijing, Liao hesitated to push forward.

literal: Was it not because the Yellow River lay ahead and the three garrisons behind, and careful counsel at the moment could not permit otherwise?
idiomatic: With the Yellow River ahead and the three prefectures behind, cautious planning at the crisis point left no other choice.

literal: The two camps, twelve palaces, one office, and five capitals had troops totaling one million six hundred forty-two thousand eight hundred.
idiomatic: Two imperial camps, twelve palaces, one office, and five capitals together fielded 1,642,800 troops.

literal: Palace ding, great chieftains, all tribes, Zhongjing, subordinate prefectures, and subject peoples were not included.
idiomatic: Palace levies, great chieftains, tribal hosts, Zhongjing, head-of-household domains, and subject troops lay outside this tally.

literal: Not deploying them lightly was how the dynasty endured long.
idiomatic: Restraint in committing them was how the dynasty lasted.
Frontier Garrison Troops

literal: Goryeo's Great Liao Affairs also records eastern-border garrison troops against Goryeo, Jurchen, and other states—showing how the frontier was held in brief, telling arrangement; one example reveals all three borders.
idiomatic: From Goryeo's record of Great Liao Affairs we also learn eastern garrisons facing Goryeo and Jurchen—a concise frontier layout from which all three borders can be inferred.

literal: From Eastern Capital to the Yalu's northwest peaks as the border: Huanglong Prefecture regular troops five thousand.
idiomatic: The Eastern Capital frontier to the Yalu's northwest ridge: 5,000 regulars at Huanglong Prefecture.
Xianzhou posted 1,000 regulars.

literal: Along the Jurchen border from Eastern Capital to the Yalu River: seventy forts in all, each holding twenty men, totaling one thousand four hundred regulars.
idiomatic: From Eastern Capital along the Jurchen line to the Yalu stood seventy forts with twenty men each—1,400 regulars in all.

literal: Laiyuan City, Xuanyi Army, eight camps: Crown Prince Camp regular troops three hundred.
idiomatic: At Laiyuan's Xuanyi Army eight camps, the Crown Prince Camp held 300 regulars.
Great Camp: 600 militia levies of regulars.

literal: Pu Prefecture Camp regular troops, 200 ding.
idiomatic: Pu Prefecture Camp: 200 militia levies of regulars.
New Camp: 500 militia levies of regulars.
Jiata Camp: 500 militia levies of regulars.
Wanghai City garrisoned 300 militia levies of regulars.
Liubai Camp: 400 militia levies of regulars.
Woye Camp: 1,000 militia levies of regulars.
Shenhu City garrisoned 10,000 militia levies of regulars.
The post was founded in Dakang year 10.

literal: Right: one prefecture, one zhou, two cities, seventy forts, eight camps—regular troops totaling twenty-two thousand.
idiomatic: Totals: one prefecture, one zhou, two cities, seventy forts, eight camps—22,000 regular troops.
